steps.label: What hormones do
steps.why: A hormone reaches every cell in the blood but only changes the ones carrying its receptor, and that is what makes it specific.
common_mistakes: Writing that hormones act on all cells. They act only on target cells.
Splitting hormones by gland instead of by solubility.
steps.memory_tip: The receptor decides the target, not the blood supply.
steps.margin_note: Set up the two-type split in the first three lines.

Based on solubility, hormones are of two

steps.label: Lipid insoluble hormones
steps.why: A hormone that cannot cross the membrane must deliver its message at the surface and let something else carry it inward.
common_mistakes: Letting these hormones enter the cell. They cannot cross the membrane.
steps.memory_tip: It cannot get in, so it knocks at the door: a membrane receptor.
lines: They bind to membrane bound receptors on
the surface of the target cell.
The receptor stimulates a G protein.

steps.label: The second messenger
steps.why: One hormone molecule makes many cAMP molecules and each of those starts more reactions, so a faint outside signal becomes a strong inside one.
common_mistakes: Calling cAMP the first messenger. The hormone is first, cAMP is second.
steps.memory_tip: Hormone outside, cAMP inside: the second messenger.
steps.margin_note: Name the enzyme, the messenger and an example.

steps.label: Lipid soluble hormones
steps.why: A hormone that can pass straight through the membrane needs no messenger: it acts on the genes itself.
common_mistakes: Giving these hormones membrane receptors. Their receptors are inside the cell.
steps.memory_tip: It walks in and goes to the genes.
steps.margin_note: Diffuse in, bind inside, act on the genes.
